10.1.summary:
Marcus is talking to himself, asking when he will finally become the person he wants to be: simple, whole, honest all the way through, and kind. He wants to stop needing more time, a better place, nicer weather or easier company in order to be content.

The aim is to accept that what you have now is enough, that it comes from the gods and from the order of the universe, which holds everything together and recycles it into new things. Someone like that could live alongside gods and people without finding fault with them and without deserving blame.
10.1.today: It's the familiar thought that you'll be happy once you've got the new job, the holiday, the bigger flat or the right friends. Marcus asks whether you could be content with this afternoon, exactly as it is, before any of that arrives.

10.2.summary: A step-by-step test for what to allow yourself. First consider what your body needs simply as a living thing, and go along with it as long as it doesn't damage you as an animal. Then consider what your animal side wants, and allow that as long as it doesn't make you worse as a reasoning being. And since being rational also means being social, what you owe to others is part of the test. Follow these rules and don't fret over anything else.

10.3.summary:
Anything that happens to you is either something you can bear or something you can't. If you can bear it, bear it without complaining. If you can't, don't complain either, because it will finish you off and then come to an end itself.

The twist is that you can bear far more than you think. Anything whose weight depends on your own opinion of it becomes bearable once you tell yourself that carrying it is in your interest, or simply your duty.
10.3.today: A long night with a sick child, a hard final month on a project, a slow recovery after an injury: much of the weight comes from the story you tell about it. Thinking 'this is my job right now' often makes it lighter than 'why is this happening to me'.

10.4.summary: When someone gets something wrong, correct them kindly and show them where they went astray. If you can't get through to them, look first at how you went about it and blame yourself. Or better still, don't blame anyone at all, not even yourself, and let it go.
10.4.today: Think of explaining something to a relative who has shared a dubious article, or to a new colleague who keeps making the same mistake. Patience works better than scorn, and if it doesn't land, try a different approach instead of writing them off.

10.5.summary: Whatever happens to you was woven into the order of things long before you arrived. Marcus pictures cause and effect as a thread spun from all eternity, with your life and everything that befalls it part of the same fabric. The point is acceptance, not gloom: nothing that comes your way is random, and none of it was singled out to spite you.

10.6.summary:
Whether the universe is ordered by a purpose or is just chance, Marcus starts from two facts. You are a part of a larger whole, and you are related to other people, who share the same nature and the same reason.

The first means you can accept what comes your way, since nothing that serves the whole truly harms a part of it. The second means you should never act against others, but put your effort into the common good. Live like that and life runs smoothly, just as a good citizen thrives by serving their city and accepting whatever role it gives them.
10.6.today: A nurse handed an unwanted night shift, or the volunteer given the dull job at the school fair, can treat it as their share of something larger instead of a personal injustice, and still put their effort into doing it well for everyone else.

10.7.summary:
Everything in the universe must eventually break down, but Marcus insists this means change, not evil. It would be absurd for nature to build its own parts to suffer harm, and just as absurd, even if you think of nature as blind process, to be outraged when things do what they were always made to do.

When something dissolves, its elements go back into the whole and become something else. Even your body is largely borrowed: the stuff in it came from recent meals and breaths, not from the day you were born. So its changing is less of a loss than it seems.

10.8.summary:
Marcus names the qualities he wants to live by: good, modest, truthful, rational, even-tempered and big-hearted. If you slip, return to them quickly. Being rational means close attention, even-tempered means accepting your lot willingly, and big-hearted means rising above pleasure, pain, fame and death.

The point is to be these things, not to be called them. Carrying on as you are, mauled by life, is like the wounded arena fighters who begged to live one more day only to face the same beasts. If you can't hold on to these qualities, retreat to a quiet corner where you can, or even leave life calmly. A fig tree does a fig tree's work; a person should do a person's.
10.8.today: You might want to be the patient parent, the honest colleague, the friend who listens. The test is whether you are those things on an ordinary Tuesday evening when nobody's watching, not whether people describe you that way in a birthday card.

10.9.summary:
Ordinary life wears your principles away day by day: entertainment, conflict, panic, sluggishness, being at others' beck and call. Marcus warns himself how much he takes for granted without thinking it through.

The remedy is to handle each task so that you get better at the practical side while still thinking clearly, with a quiet confidence that comes from understanding things, neither flaunted nor hidden. He wants to see each thing for what it is: what it's made of, how long it lasts, where it fits, and who can give it or take it away.
10.9.today: The modern list might be streaming shows, office politics, the news alert that makes your stomach drop, the mid-afternoon slump and an inbox that sets your agenda. Any of them can push your values out of mind before lunchtime.

10.10.summary: Pride in a catch depends on what you've caught. A spider is pleased with a fly, a hunter with a hare or a bear, a general with a defeated people. Marcus includes himself here: the Sarmatians were a people he spent years fighting on Rome's Danube frontier. Look honestly at the motives, he says, and the conqueror is only a grander kind of robber.

10.11.summary:
Train yourself to notice how everything is constantly turning into something else. Nothing builds largeness of spirit like this habit. Someone who grasps that they will soon leave everything behind stops clutching, and concentrates on two things: acting justly in what they're doing now, and accepting whatever happens to them.

Such a person doesn't spare a thought for what others say or think or do against them. They drop the busy distractions and want only to follow the straight path of reason, which for Marcus is the same as following God.

10.12.summary: There's no need for anxious second-guessing when you can work out what ought to be done. If the way is clear, take it calmly and don't look back. If it isn't, stop and get the best advice you can. If obstacles come up, keep going as well as you can, holding to what seems right. If you do fail, at least let it be while attempting the right thing. Following reason makes you calm and active at once, cheerful and steady.
10.12.today: Facing a career decision or a difficult conversation, it's easy to lie awake at 2am running through every possible outcome. The plainer route is to act if you know what's right, ask someone wise if you don't, and then stop chewing it over.

10.13.summary:
First thing each morning, ask whether it makes any difference to you that someone else does what is just and right. It makes none: your own goodness is not on loan from anyone else's.

Then remember what the people who hand out praise and blame so grandly are really like: how they behave in bed and at the table, what they chase and avoid, and how they steal, not with their hands but by misusing their mind, the very part that could have made them faithful, modest, truthful and happy. Their verdicts are worth little.

10.14.summary: Someone who has learned well and is humble says to nature, which gives everything and takes it all back: give what you like, take back what you like. And they say it not as a show of toughness or pride, but obediently and gladly, out of real contentment with the way things work.

10.15.summary:
Not much of your life is left, so live as though you were on a mountain, away from it all. Where you live makes no difference if you treat the whole world as your city.

Let people see someone who genuinely lives by nature. If they can't stand it, let them kill you. Marcus means it: that would be better than living the way most people do.

10.16.summary: Stop discussing what a good person should be like and just be one. Marcus is cutting through his own habit of reflecting and theorising about virtue. Philosophy, for him, is worth nothing unless it shows up in how you actually behave today.
10.16.today: It's the difference between reading one more book about habits and actually going for the run, or between posting about kindness and ringing the friend who's having a hard week.

10.17.summary: Keep the whole picture in view: all of time and all of matter. Against that, any single thing is as small as a fig seed in size and as brief as one turn of a gimlet, a little hand drill, in time. The exercise is about perspective. Whatever looms large today shrinks once you see where it sits.

10.18.summary: Look at anything around you and notice that it is already coming apart, changing, rotting or scattering. Everything is made by nature to die. Seeing decay already at work, instead of waiting to be surprised by it, loosens your grip on things and makes their loss less of a shock.
10.18.today: The new car is already losing value, the phone is already heading for obsolescence, and the flowers on the table are already wilting. Seeing that plainly can make it easier to enjoy them without clinging.

10.19.summary: Picture the powerful in their ordinary moments: eating, sleeping, having sex, using the toilet. Then picture them lording it over others or scolding from on high. Not long ago they were slaves to all sorts of people and appetites, and before long they'll be dead. The exercise takes the shine off anyone who seems grand, and makes arrogance, theirs or your own, hard to take seriously.
10.19.today: When a boss, a celebrity or a loud online commentator seems intimidating, remember they also queue for coffee, fall asleep on the sofa and argue about the washing-up. It's hard to feel small next to someone you can picture in their dressing gown.

10.20.summary: Whatever the nature of the universe brings to something is good for it, and good at the very moment it arrives. Marcus is asking himself to trust the timing of events as well as the events themselves, instead of wishing they had come later, sooner or not at all.

10.21.summary:
Marcus borrows lines of poetry about the earth loving the rain and the sky loving to send it, and applies them to the universe, which loves to bring about whatever comes next. His reply is simple: then I love what you love.

He also plays on a Greek turn of phrase in which 'it loves to happen' just means 'it tends to happen'. Accepting events becomes something warmer than resignation, a kind of agreement with the way things unfold.

10.22.summary: There are only three possibilities. You stay where you are, and you're already used to it. You leave, which was your own choice. Or you die, having done your duty. There's nothing beyond these, so be cheerful. Marcus is shrinking the range of things to worry about down to a few options, each of them acceptable.

10.23.summary: This place is no different from any other. Life on a mountaintop, by the sea or anywhere else is the same, because what matters is how you live, not where. Marcus recalls Plato's image of living inside the city walls as if in a shepherd's fold on a mountain: the solitude you want can come with you.
10.23.today: The dream of escaping to a cottage by the sea or a cabin in the hills often assumes a new place will make you a new person. The calm you're after is just as available on the bus or at your desk.

10.24.summary: A set of questions for checking on your own mind. What is it doing for me right now? What am I turning it into, and what am I using it for? Is it empty of good sense? Has it cut itself off from other people? Has it become so tangled up with the body that it just goes wherever the body's wants take it?
10.24.today: A useful check during a long day of screens: is my attention going somewhere I chose, or has it been carried off by hunger, tiredness and the next notification?

10.25.summary: A slave who flees his master is a runaway, and the law of the universe is a master too, so whoever breaks it is a runaway. Marcus goes further. When you grieve, rage or fear, you're objecting to something past, present or future that has been assigned by whatever rules all things, which is law itself, giving each person their due. So giving way to fear, grief or anger is a kind of desertion.

10.26.summary: Life comes from processes you never see. A seed is planted, then something else takes over and forms a child. A child swallows food, and some unseen power turns it into perception, movement and strength. Marcus invites wonder at these hidden forces. You can't see them with your eyes, any more than you can see the force that makes things fall or rise, yet they are just as plain.

10.27.summary: History keeps repeating with a new cast. Picture entire royal courts from the past: Hadrian's, that of Antoninus Pius (Marcus's adoptive father), and those of Philip of Macedon, Alexander the Great and Croesus, the famously rich king of Lydia. They were all the same play we watch now, only with different actors. Seeing this takes the novelty and the melodrama out of the present.
10.27.today: The office reshuffle, the family feud, the gossip about who's in and who's out: someone has played every one of these scenes before. Recognising the script makes it easier not to get swept up in it.

10.28.summary:
Someone who is aggrieved by what happens is like a pig at the sacrifice, kicking and squealing. So is the person lying silently in bed, lamenting the ties that bind us all.

Everyone has to go along with what happens. Only rational beings get to go along with it willingly. Resisting doesn't change the outcome, it only adds the squealing.

10.29.summary: With each thing you do, stop and ask: is death really so terrible because it would take this away from me? The honest answer often shows how little the activity matters, and how much of your fear of death is attached to things that don't deserve it.
10.29.today: Try it mid-scroll, during a petty argument about whose turn it was to empty the dishwasher, or while refreshing your inbox for the fifth time. Few of these are things you'd mourn losing.

10.30.summary:
When someone's fault annoys you, look straight at your own similar faults, such as treating money, pleasure or a bit of reputation as if they were truly good. That quickly takes the heat out of your anger.

It helps, too, to remember that the other person is acting under compulsion: given what they believe, what else could they do? And if you can, help free them from the mistaken belief that drives them.
10.30.today: When a colleague grabs the credit, remember the times you angled for a mention yourself. When a driver cuts you up, recall the days you were the one in a rush. Anger fades fast once you spot the same weakness at home.

10.31.summary:
When you see someone, think of a similar person from the past who is now gone: Marcus pairs people he knows, including philosophers, with others who have died. When you look at yourself, think of the emperors before you. Where are they now? Nowhere, or nobody knows where.

Seen this way, human affairs are smoke. So why not pass your own brief time in an orderly way? Everything that happens is material for your reason to work on. Digest it all, as a strong stomach takes in any food or a fire turns whatever is thrown on it into flame.

10.32.summary: Make sure nobody can truthfully say you are not straightforward or not good. If anyone thinks so, let them be wrong. This is entirely up to you, since nobody can stop you being good and simple. Marcus adds a hard line: decide not to go on living unless you are such a person, because reason gives you no grounds to live otherwise.

10.33.summary:
In any situation, ask what the most reasonable thing to do or say is. You can always do it, so make no excuses. Doing what fits your nature should feel to you the way luxury feels to a pleasure-seeker.

Physical things get blocked, but reason can work its way through any obstacle, as naturally as fire rises or a stone falls. Obstacles touch only the body or, if you let them, your opinions. Other things are made worse by damage, but a person can become better by handling misfortune well. Nothing harms a citizen that doesn't harm the city, and nothing harms the city that doesn't harm its law and order.
10.33.today: A cancelled train, a project scrapped at the last minute, a diagnosis that changes your plans: each closes some doors, but the question of how you respond stays open. That part is always yours to work with.

10.34.summary:
If your principles are sound, even a familiar line of poetry is enough to free you from grief and fear. Marcus quotes Homer: people are like leaves the wind scatters. Your children are leaves. So are those who praise you, curse you or sneer behind your back, and those who will carry your reputation into the future.

They all spring up, fall and are replaced by new growth. Everything is brief, yet you chase and flee things as if they would last forever. Soon you will close your eyes, and before long someone will be mourning the person who buried you.

10.35.summary:
A healthy eye sees whatever is there instead of demanding only green things. Healthy hearing and smell take in everything, and a healthy stomach deals with all food, like a mill grinding whatever it's given.

A healthy mind should likewise be ready for whatever happens. Insisting 'let my children live' or 'let everyone praise what I do' is like an eye that wants only green, or teeth that will only chew soft food. Even the dearest wishes become a weakness when your peace depends on them.
10.35.today: Demanding that everything goes smoothly, that the review is glowing, the holiday sunny and the children always well, is like living on mashed potato. A sturdy mind can digest bad news along with the good.

10.36.summary:
No one is so lucky that nobody will be glad at their deathbed. Even a good and wise person will have someone thinking: at last we're free of the schoolmaster, who never scolded us but made us feel judged. Most of us give people more reasons than that.

Remembering this makes leaving easier. Why cling to a life where even those you worked for may want you gone? But don't leave resentful. Stay kind and gentle, and part from people as easily as a peaceful death separates soul from body: nature joined you to them, and now nature is undoing the tie.

10.37.summary: Whenever anyone does something, get into the habit of asking what they're trying to achieve by it. But start with yourself, and examine your own motives first. Asking about others helps you understand them; asking about yourself keeps you honest about why you do what you do.
10.37.today: Before firing off the email, posting the photo or volunteering for the high-profile project, ask why. Sometimes the honest answer is to look good, and noticing that is half the work.

10.38.summary: What really drives you is the hidden thing inside, your mind and reason. That is what persuades and moves you, that is life, and that, you might say, is the person. When you think about yourself, leave out the body and its limbs. They're tools like an axe, except that they happen to be attached. Without the mind directing them, they're as useless as a weaver's shuttle, a pen or a driver's whip with no one using them.
